highlights.text: to guard oneself and to be alert/vigilant
ḥadhira / yaḥdharu / ḥadharan — to be cautious or wary.
ḥadhirūn means "fearful" (khāʾifūn).
"Beware of our spears, beware!"
rousing someone to something, and low-lying ground

its arriving/coming, and its being witnessed or present.
ḥaḍarat al-ṣalāt (the prayer arrived)

Shāhid from Ḥassān ("a populous ḥāḍir…")

her words mean that the lie has swerved off and the truth is plain.

highlights.note: a hadith of Samura ibn Jundub

highlights.text: A violent wind carrying dust and gravel; also said of scattered fine hail and snow.
Anything cast into a fire, firewood or otherwise. Qurʾān: "You and what you serve apart from God are the ḥaṣab of Jahannam."
Ibn Manẓūr records two readings: a punishment that pelts them with stones of sijjīl, or a wind so strong it tears up the gravel.

gathering something together.

highlights.text: gathering together, confining, and preventing.
**al-iḥṣār — a pilgrim being kept from the House by illness or the like.**
Ibn Fāris glosses ḥaṣīr as the place of confinement, a prison.
**al-ḥaṣūr — a man who does not go in to women.**
as in Labīd's phrase "standing at the door of the ḥaṣīr."
أَحْصَى (aḥṣā), "to encompass / comprehend fully."

Shāhid: al-Aʿshā, "you are not the more numerous among them, for might belongs to the more numerous."
bringing a thing down from a height.
he reports an explanation given by others ("they said"): it means "O God, put our burdens (awzār) down off us."
A verse describes a fair, plump woman, full in the haunches, "maḥṭūṭat al-matnayn," not worn by bearing children one after another.
highlights.note: unattributed verse, on the "pressed down" sense

highlights.text: fuel — al-waqūd, i.e. firewood/kindling.
al-ḥaṭab = "firewood" (a well-known word). Verb: ḥaṭaba – yaḥṭibu – ḥaṭban, "to gather firewood."
Imruʾ al-Qays' line where children say "come, let's gather firewood until the game arrives."
An anonymous verse describes a greedy, lazy man who cries from hunger yet "neither gathers firewood for the people nor gives them water"
Ibn Fāris reports that scholars ("they said") read this as a kināya — a figurative, euphemistic expression — for namīma, talebearing/slander, not literal wood-carrying.
ḥaṭm is breaking something, of the same order as hashm
"Let not Solomon and his troops crush you" (27:18).
the name given to the blazing fire (al-jaḥīm)
what crumbles apart because it has dried out.
"as though in his belly there were an oven."
share, and good fortune.
a share or portion; fortune (al-jadd).
prevention / forbidding (al-manʿ).
the thing is maḥẓūr ("forbidden/withheld").
The person who builds such an enclosure is called al-muḥtaẓir.
the deed-nullifying sense (ḥabṭ) derives from belly-bloat (ḥabaṭ): as the bloated animal perishes, so the hypocrite's deed comes to nothing
highlights.note: al-Azharī's own view, bridging "bloat" and "deed made void"

highlights.text: ḥabiṭa (ḥabṭ, ḥubūṭ) = one did a deed then spoiled it; God made it void (aḥbaṭahu).
Cited from Revelation: "so He made their deeds void" (fa-aḥbaṭa aʿmālahum).
a horse swollen in the flanks (faras ḥabiṭ al-quṣayrā; cited with al-Jaʿdī's verse).
Among what spring grows is that which kills by bloat, or nearly so.
Ibn al-Athīr derives this abstract usage directly from the animal sense — the beast that over-eats and dies.
(2) the grain of anything that bears grain, and (3) shortness.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's grain and shortness origins

highlights.text: holding fast and staying fixed
Ibn Fāris derives al-ḥubb and al-maḥabba, "love", from this sense: aḥabbahu means that one held fast to the thing.
al-ḥabb is the familiar grain of wheat and barley.
Ṭarafa: "when she laughs she shows ḥabab, like musk-sweet saliva with cool water."
The Prophet said of certain people that "they come out of the Fire and sprout as the ḥibba sprouts in the silt carried by the flood."
making something firm/well-knit along a stretched, extended, regular course
hubuk means "tara'iq" -- tracks, paths, or streaks (singular: habikah)
something extends or stretches out.
ḥabl — a rope or halter (plural ḥibāl). This is the plain, well-known sense.
ḥabl — a covenant or pact. Ibn Fāris marks this explicitly as the figurative extension of the rope.
a line of al-Aʿshā about a traveller passing from tribe to tribe: the "ropes" of one tribe carry the rider along until she reaches the next
in a line of Labīd describing his mount, this means the pasterns of the animal, so called because that is where the hobbling rope sits.
**a mark or trace left in something, associated with beauty and splendour.**
حِبْر / حَبْر (ḥibr, ḥabr) is the man who writes with ink — that is, the learned man — plural أَحْبَار (aḥbār).
الحَبْرَة (al-ḥabra) is joy. He cites Q 30:15, "so they, in a meadow, are made glad (yuḥbarūn)."
a line of Ibn Aḥmar: "we wore its comeliness until we were called to account."
He quotes a ḥadīth about a man coming out of the Fire "whose ḥibr and sibr have gone,"
to hold something back, to restrain or detain it.
the verb habasa / habastuhu habsan means "I detained/confined him"; the verbal noun habs simply means a detaining, a holding-back.
